assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (Katori's magic-wavelength concept, Ye's realisation of record stability and accuracy) opened a new regime of frequency metrology at the 1e-18 level and underpin tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a prospective redefinition of the second. The idea is clean, original and has lasting impact across atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice trapping scheme; Ye's group drove the strontium clock to the accuracy and stability frontier. A two-person prize is natural. Others in the field (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) contributed, but the core credit is reasonably concentrated on the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs worldwide now operate optical lattice clocks and compare them; the interpretation is stable and recognition is timely, following the 2005 prize for the comb and the 2012 prize for ion control.
uncertainties: Credit for early lattice-clock demonstrations versus later accuracy records may be contested by other groups.
Ye's association with John Hall's laboratory overlaps with my own documented connection to that laboratory; I note this as a potential perceived connection, not a conflict I regard as decisive.
I have not independently verified the details of priority claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum computing with trapped ions and its experimental realisation by Blatt's group provided the first concrete, physically complete architecture for quantum gates and simulation. Very high originality and enduring impact on the entire quantum-technology field.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the theoretical originators; Blatt is a leading experimental realiser of gates, entanglement and algorithms with trapped ions. Wineland and Haroche already received the 2012 prize, and Monroe, Wineland and others share experimental credit, so the experimental side is somewhat open.
assessment.maturity: Trapped-ion processors have been demonstrated for over two decades by several groups and are commercially deployed. Confirmation is strong and recognition is mature, if somewhat overlapping with earlier prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize scope could be argued against novelty of recognition.
Experimental credit is shared with several groups outside the proposed trio (e.g. Monroe, Wineland), so the fairest experimental laureate is not obvious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson at the LHC was a landmark confirmation of the electroweak symmetry-breaking mechanism and of the Standard Model. Importance and clarity are exceptional; the 2013 prize recognised the theory but not the experimental discovery.
assessment.attribution: The three named individuals are widely credited as founding spokespersons and architects of the ATLAS and CMS collaborations, which is a defensible configuration within the three-laureate limit given the collaborations' size. Credit to accelerator builders and other leaders is necessarily excluded.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation by two experiments and subsequent coupling measurements make the discovery very mature; recognition of the experimental side is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Allocating a collaboration-scale discovery to three individuals is inherently contested.
Whether the Academy would favour founders versus discovery-year spokespersons or an institutional focus is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene combined a theoretical prediction of flat bands with experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity, launching moire quantum materials and twistronics. Highly original and a very active field with clear conceptual impact.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic-angle flat bands; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. That is a clean theory plus experiment trio. Others such as Dean, Yacoby and Young also contributed to follow-up work.
assessment.maturity: Strongly replicated across many laboratories, yet the origin of superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated, so the fundamental interpretation is not yet settled. Recognition could be timely or slightly early.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity remains unresolved.
Other twisted-graphene experimental groups (e.g. Dean, Young, Yacoby) may merit credit that the trio cannot include.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision tool for measuring gravity, rotation, the fine-structure constant and for tests of the equivalence principle, with clear connections to laser cooling and optical techniques I know well. Strong originality and growing application impact.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated early atom interferometers, Bordé developed the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer and theory, and Kasevich pioneered high-precision gravimetry and gyroscopes. Others (Chu, Mlynek, Keith, Rasel) also hold claims; the proposed trio is defensible but not uniquely determined.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed, with commercial gravimeters and large-scale experiments under way; the decisive fundamental-physics results still lie ahead, but the technique is established.
uncertainties: Chu's prior prize for laser cooling may complicate how the interferometry credit is allocated.
Credit between early demonstrations and later precision applications is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision (three-step) model and its quantum theory of high-harmonic generation explain strong-field ionisation, HHG and attosecond pulse generation in simple physical terms. Prior prize work (2023) recognised attosecond experiments but not Corkum's model; the conceptual clarity and impact are exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Corkum and Schafer formulated the semiclassical recollision picture, and Lewenstein gave the quantum strong-field approximation. Kulander also shares Schafer-era credit, and Krausz and L'Huillier already hold the 2023 prize, so the fair configuration depends on how the Academy treats that overlap.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in countless experiments and widely used; mature, though the 2023 prize may have reduced the perceived need for a further attosecond-related award.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 attosecond prize may reduce the case for recognition.
Priority between Corkum, Kulander-Schafer and Lewenstein is a matter of record that I cannot resolve here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity QED interfaces between single atoms and photons enable quantum networks, deterministic photon-atom gates and state transfer, forming the foundation of light-matter quantum interfaces. As someone working on optical quantum memories I see this as important and conceptually clear, though technology still evolving.
assessment.attribution: Kimble pioneered strong coupling and the quantum-network vision, Rempe achieved atom-photon state transfer and single-photon sources, and Cirac with Zoller supplied the network proposal. Cirac also appears in B033, so the same person may be preferred in only one prize.
assessment.maturity: Core demonstrations are well confirmed, but scalable quantum networks are not yet established; recognition may be somewhat early for the network aspect and mature for the cavity-QED basis.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for cavity QED (Haroche) and with B033 (Cirac) complicates the configuration.
Whether network-level impact is yet sufficient is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for quantum-enhanced measurement beat the standard quantum limit and was deployed in gravitational-wave detectors, a direct realisation of the idea that sensing is limited by measurement accuracy. The idea is original, and the application in LIGO gives lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-state enhancement of interferometers, Kimble made the first squeezed-light experiments, and Mavalvala led squeezing implementation in LIGO. Schnabel's GEO600 work and other early experimenters (Slusher, Wu) also have significant claims; the fourth name is excluded here.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in operating gravitational-wave observatories; mature, with continuing improvements. Recognition would be timely in view of LIGO's 2017 prize, but the credit chain from theory to detector is long.
uncertainties: Excluded credited names (e.g. Schnabel) and early experimenters not on the list may deserve credit.
